news_title: CAQM directs MCG to prosecute official for failing to implement dust mitigation measures
efet_title: CAQM directs MCG to prosecute official for failing to implement dust mitigation measures
efet_body:
CAQM directs MCG to prosecute official for failing to implement dust mitigation measures
The examination found heaps of loose soil and construction and demolition dust lying unattended alongside road stretches.
Updated on: Nov 6, 2026, 20:59:26 IST
PTI
Prefer HT
on Google
Share via
Copy link
The CAQM has directed the Municipal Corporation of Gurugram to prosecute an executive engineer and other officials for allegedly failing to ensure implementation of dust mitigation measures at various levels, sources said on Friday.
Sheoran and others will be prosecuted in front of a jurisdictional judicial magistrate under Section 14 (2) of the Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021. (PTI)
The development comes after the MCG, in a letter dated October 30 to the Urban Local Bodies Department, Haryana, recommended disciplinary action against Executive Engineer Surender Sheoran for allegedly mismanaging mechanised road-sweeping machines, and ensuring effective dust-managing operations.
Also read |
GRAP-II pollution curbs imposed in Delhi-NCR as air quality dips further
Sheoran and others will be prosecuted in front of a jurisdictional judicial magistrate under Section 14 (2) of the Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021.
The section states, "The offence under this Act shall be non-cognizable and triable by the Jurisdictional Judicial Magistrate of the First Class, who shall not take cognisance of the offence except upon a complaint made by the Commission or any officer authorised by the Commission in this behalf."
Also read |
Supreme Court reluctant to shut schools or shift classes online amid Delhi's worsening air quality
The failure to implement dust mitigation measures first came to light in December last year during a CAQM inspection of 125 road stretches under MCG jurisdiction. Sources said that the examination found 34 stretches with high visible dust, and 58 with moderate visible dust, according to sources.
In February this year, the CAQM conducted another inspection after receiving a complaint regarding accumulation of dust and municipal solid waste in Gurugram's sectors 49, 50, 70, 73, 74, and 75. The examination found heaps of loose soil and construction and demolition dust lying unattended alongside road stretches.
Then, in October, to further ascertain dust mitigation measures, CAQM carried out examinations of 52 road stretches and found more than 250 instances of violations, including high visible dust on roads. Out of this, 174 violations were found on the road stretches under MCG jurisdiction.
According to sources, after the MCG commissioner appeared in front of the CAQM on November 3 regarding the issue, it was decided to hold Sheoran and other officials accountable for the above-mentioned violations.

Things to check before buying Diwali mithai
No Diwali is complete without a box of mithai, but every year, the festive rush also brings a darker side. With demand for milk, ghee, khoya and paneer shooting up, food safety teams across the country conduct raids and seize large quantities of adulterated products. That doesn’t mean you should give up on sweets, only that it pays to be a little careful before you buy and serve them. You don’t need a laboratory, since a few simple checks at home can help you spot warning signs. Here are five easy ways to pick safer sweets for your family.
2
/
6
Start with the shop and the label
The first check happens before you even taste anything. Buy from a licensed, trusted shop, and look for the FSSAI licence number displayed at the counter or printed on the packaging. For packaged sweets, check the manufacturing and expiry or best-before dates. Food safety officials have also advised consumers to check these details before buying. If a shop looks unhygienic, or the sweets are sitting uncovered in the sun, that’s a good reason to walk away, no matter how tempting they look.
3
/
6
Use your eyes, nose and fingers
Your senses are a surprisingly good first filter. Be wary of sweets that look unnaturally bright, especially in yellow and orange, because that can be a sign of synthetic colours. Smell them too, since a strange, sour or soapy smell and a bitter taste are warning signs. For mawa, try the palm test. Pure mawa feels slightly oily and grainy, while mawa that feels sticky, powdery or dry may have been mixed with other things. If something seems off, don’t eat it.
4
/
6
Try the iodine test for starch
Starch is sometimes added to mawa, paneer and ghee to increase their weight. FSSAI’s suggested home test uses tincture of iodine, which you can get at any chemist. For khoya or paneer, boil a small sample with water, let it cool, and add two or three drops of iodine. If it turns blue or blue-black, starch is present. For ghee, put half a teaspoon in a clear bowl and add a few drops. A blue colour means starch. Never taste the sample afterwards, because iodine is not meant to be eaten.
5
/
6
Choose smarter and buy less
Milk-based sweets are perishable, so buy only what you need, keep them refrigerated and eat them within a day or two. Choose sweets with less artificial colouring, or go for options like dry fruit barfis, ladoos made with dates and nuts, or sweets you make at home. Making a few at home also gives you complete control over what goes into them. If you suspect that a sweet is adulterated, don’t eat it, and report the shop to your state’s food safety department.
A few minutes of checking can make the festive season safer and a lot more enjoyable. Because the best sweets aren’t just the ones that look good in the box, they’re the ones that you can feel confident about sharing with the people you love.
6
/
6
Disclaimer:
This article is intended for general informational purposes only. Home tests are only indicative and can detect just a few kinds of adulteration, so they cannot guarantee that a sweet is safe. Tincture of iodine is poisonous if swallowed, so keep it away from children and never eat a tested sample. Be careful when using a flame for the foil test. If you feel unwell after eating sweets, seek medical advice.

Food safety must be built into business operations, not treated as a compliance checklist: FSSAI's Satyen Kumar Panda
Speaking at the 2nd Edition of ET FoodXP 2026, Satyen Kumar Panda, Advisor, FSSAI, urged food businesses to adopt preventive safety systems, strengthen transparency and ensure accountability across the supply chain. He highlighted emerging regulatory priorities around food labelling, ingredient safety and e-commerce, stressing that stronger standards can build consumer confidence and support sustainable industry growth.

India's rapidly expanding food industry must treat
food safety
as a fundamental business responsibility rather than a regulatory obligation, as
consumer trust
becomes increasingly critical to sustainable growth, said Satyen Kumar Panda, Advisor, Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (
FSSAI
).
Delivering a keynote address titled How Can Stronger Food Standards Build Consumer Trust and Unlock Industry Growth? at the 2nd Edition of ET FoodXP 2026, Panda emphasised that the sector's growth potential would depend on its ability to maintain consistent safety, quality and transparency across products and distribution channels.
With food consumption patterns evolving, distribution networks becoming faster and new brands entering the market, Panda said consumers have access to greater choice than ever before. However, he cautioned that expanding business opportunities also bring greater responsibility.
According to him, food businesses cannot sustain growth without consumer confidence, making stronger standards and effective regulation essential to the industry's long-term development.
"Standards do not stand in the way of growth," Panda said, arguing that robust regulatory frameworks create the conditions in which responsible businesses can expand and consumers can make informed purchasing decisions.
He urged manufacturers, retailers, distributors and foodservice operators to move beyond compliance-driven approaches and integrate safety considerations into sourcing, formulation, production and delivery.
Food safety requires coordination between central and state authorities
Explaining India's regulatory framework, Panda highlighted the shared responsibilities of central and state authorities in enforcing food safety requirements.
He noted that FSSAI was established under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, with the objective of creating a coordinated approach to
food regulation
across the country.
While the central regulatory framework establishes standards and requirements, state authorities play a major role in enforcement and responding to food safety incidents.
Panda stressed that businesses must understand this division of responsibility, particularly as their operations expand across multiple states.
He also referred to changes in food business licensing arrangements and efforts to improve the identification of licensing jurisdictions.
According to him, greater clarity around the origin and regulatory jurisdiction of food products can help consumers identify the appropriate authority when raising complaints or reporting suspected violations.
For businesses operating across geographically dispersed supply chains, this makes regulatory awareness and coordination increasingly important.
Emerging regulations to focus on labelling, ingredients and product safety
Panda outlined several regulatory developments that food businesses should closely monitor, particularly in the areas of labelling, ingredient safety and product classification.
He highlighted precautionary allergen labelling as an emerging area of international regulatory attention.
Unlike conventional allergen declarations, which identify allergens present in a product, precautionary labelling addresses potential risks associated with unintended allergen presence.
Panda indicated that such developments would require businesses to strengthen their understanding of ingredient sourcing, manufacturing processes and potential contamination risks.
He also referred to ongoing international discussions concerning food fraud, specialised dietary products and food intended for infants and young children.
India's participation in international food standard-setting mechanisms, including engagement with the Codex Alimentarius framework, was highlighted as an important part of regulatory alignment.
Panda said emerging international requirements could influence how food businesses approach product development and compliance.
Domestically, he pointed to continuing discussions around front-of-pack nutrition labelling, which has attracted attention as consumers seek clearer information about the nutritional composition of packaged foods.
